analysis.one_liner: Restricts bulk sales of federally insured delinquent mortgages, forcing more loan modifications and keeping foreclosed homes off the investor market.
analysis.headline: Introduced with the Senate Democratic leader among its cosponsors, the bill has sat in the Banking Committee since January 2026 with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When borrowers fall behind on FHA or Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac mortgages, the agencies sometimes sell those loans in bulk to private investors. This bill would tighten the rules around those sales: lenders would have to exhaust all options to modify the loan first, borrowers would get 90 days' written notice, buyers would have to offer the same payment-relief programs the government offers, and most foreclosed homes would have to be sold to people who will live in them, nonprofits, or affordable-rental landlords rather than investor flippers. It also creates a 'first look' period giving owner-occupants and nonprofits the first chance to buy FHA foreclosures before investors.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners who fall behind on FHA or Fannie/Freddie mortgages, who would get more chances to modify their loans before the loan is sold to an investor, clearer notice before any sale, and continuation of government-style payment relief after a sale. Neighborhoods where foreclosed homes would go to owner-occupants, nonprofits, and long-term affordable renters instead of investor portfolios, and renters whose source of income like housing vouchers must be accepted. Nonprofits, land banks, and local governments, which would get first priority and the right to buy foreclosed properties directly.

how_it_helps.text: Before any delinquent loan can be sold, all available loss mitigation — payment reduction and deferral options — must be exhausted, and the buyer must honor payment-relief terms at least as favorable as FHA or enterprise guidelines, with no fees for modifications [S2].

Borrowers and anyone on the property record must receive written notice at least 90 days before their loan is put into a bulk sale, describing the protections available and the servicer's obligations [S2].
Loans cannot be sold while a borrower is in a forbearance plan or within 90 days of leaving one [S2].

For foreclosed properties where keeping the home is impossible, 75 percent must go to owner-occupants at fair market value, to nonprofits or local governments, or to affordable rentals capped at 30 percent of income for 10 years, accepting vouchers and other lawful income sources; 'contract for deed' and lease-to-own deals that strip equity from families are banned [S2].

A new FHA 'First Look' program gives owner-occupants, pre-approved nonprofits, and government agencies an exclusive early window to buy foreclosed FHA properties at or below market value before investors can bid [S2].

Buyers must report quarterly loan outcomes and demographics, with semiannual public reports including a fair-lending analysis; agencies can seize loans back without compensation from buyers who break the rules and bar repeat violators from future sales [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Investors and funds that currently buy pools of delinquent government-backed mortgages at a discount and profit from foreclosing or reselling, who would face purchase restrictions, compliance costs, and penalties. FHA and Fannie/Freddie would get lower sale prices because buyers discount for the added obligations, which falls indirectly on the insurance fund and taxpayers. Mortgage servicers would carry new notice and reporting duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bulk loan buyers and mortgage servicers

drawbacks.text: Restrictions and compliance costs would lower the prices investors are willing to pay for delinquent loan pools, reducing the recoveries the FHA insurance fund and the mortgage enterprises receive — a cost borne by taxpayers and other FHA borrowers if the fund is shorted [S2].

The bill allows FHA sales only if the Secretary determines no other measures can keep the fund above minimum capital, which could make it harder to move troubled loans off the government's books in a downturn, concentrating delinquency risk in the fund [S2].

Many small nonprofits and land banks lack the capital or experience to buy and manage large loan pools, so priority systems may be hard to operationalize in practice despite the bill's capacity requirements [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are substantial and targeted at a specific, well-documented harm: families losing homes to investors who buy their loans at a discount and offer little help. The honest cost is that restricting who can buy these loans, and on what terms, means the government recovers less cash on each sale — a real but second-order cost compared to the foreclosures and neighborhood damage the bill aims to prevent. The design relies heavily on nonprofit and local government buyers being able to absorb volume, which is uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2026 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has had no further action while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill on January 30, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1].
The complete action history shows only introduction and committee referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled [S4].
Four senators cosponsored, all Democrats, including the Senate Majority Leader [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the investors and funds that buy pools of delinquent government-backed mortgages under the current, lighter-touch rules; nothing has changed yet for borrowers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Loan investors, for now — nothing has changed

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its predecessor-style protections restricting FHA and Fannie/Freddie bulk loan sales.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, signaling support from Senate Democratic leadership.

for.name: Sens. Tina Smith, Ron Wyden, and Jeff Merkley

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican senator
against.what_they_did: Holds the referred bill; has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — since referral in January 2026.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republican support, and the bill sits in a committee where no action has been taken.

industries.industry: Investors and funds that buy pools of delinquent government-backed mortgages
industries.note: Their business model — buying nonperforming loans at a discount and profiting through foreclosure or resale — would face purchase restrictions, mandatory payment relief, resale conditions on foreclosed homes, and loss of properties back without compensation for violations. Their gains come at the expense of families losing homes and neighborhoods absorbing vacant properties.
New certified-mail notice duties and 90-day pre-sale obligations add costs, but servicers of sold loans would face stricter conduct requirements that benefit borrowers.

industries.industry: Nonprofits, land banks, and local housing agencies
industries.note: They would get first priority in loan sales, the right to buy delinquent loans directly at prices reflecting compliance costs, and an exclusive early window on FHA foreclosures, creating a new pipeline of affordable housing inventory.

industries.industry: FHA Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund and Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac
industries.note: Lower proceeds on loan sales and slower disposition could strain the fund's capital, but fewer foreclosures and fewer claims paid also protect the fund; the bill allows sales only when capital requirements would otherwise be breached.

analysis.trajectory: A bill with no Republican cosponsors and no committee action two-thirds of the way through a Congress rarely reaches the floor; it is far more likely to die in committee at the end of 2026 than to advance, unless it is folded into a broader housing or funding package.
